title: Use of AI in Mental Health Care: Community and Mental Health Professionals Survey
study_design: Cross-sectional web-based survey with descriptive statistics and thematic analysis
population: Australian community members aged 16 years and older and mental health professionals residing in Australia
sample_size: 193 total; 107 community members and 86 mental health professionals
country_or_setting: Australia; online survey advertised on LinkedIn, Instagram, and Facebook
ai_type_application: Commercial AI tools, especially large language model chatbots such as ChatGPT, used for mental health support by community members and for professional tasks by mental health professionals
ai_exposure_intervention: Self-reported use of AI tools in the previous 6 months for mental health and well-being support or professional mental health work tasks
comparator_control_group: No formal comparator or control group; descriptive comparison between AI users and broader respondent groups/community members versus mental health professionals
mental_health_outcome: Perceived mental health support, emotional well-being support, psychological distress characteristics, and self-reported benefits, harms, and concerns from AI use
outcome_measurement_tool: Kessler 10-Item Scale (K10) for community members; AI Attitudes Scale; custom survey items on AI use, benefits, harms, and concerns
positive_effects: Community members reported AI was beneficial for quick advice when emotionally distressed, acting as a personal therapist or coach, availability, low cost compared with therapy, and privacy. Mental health professionals reported benefits for research, report and letter writing, helpfulness, and time saving. Free-text responses highlighted improved accessibility, efficiency, personalization, and potential integration with other technologies.
negative_effects_harms: Community members reported responses being too general or not personalized, uncertainty about where data was going, inaccuracy, unhelpful responses, lack of human connection, ethical/privacy concerns, and risk of misdiagnosis or missing distress signals. Mental health professionals reported outputs being too general, inaccurate, ethical concerns about professional use, risks of clinician overreliance, misuse, regulatory challenges, and data governance/security concerns.
evidence_type: Self-reported survey data with descriptive quantitative results and qualitative thematic analysis
main_finding: AI tools are already being used by a substantial minority of community members and mental health professionals in Australia. Most users perceived benefits, but around half also reported harms or concerns, especially around general/inaccurate outputs, privacy, ethics, reduced human connection, and data security.
effect_size_key_result: 28% (30/108) of community members and 43% (37/86) of mental health professionals reported AI use in the previous 6 months. Among users, 77% (23/30) of community members and 92% (34/37) of mental health professionals reported AI to be beneficial, while 47% (14/30) of community members and 51% (19/37) of mental health professionals experienced harms or concerns. Mean K10 score among community members was 22.8 (SD 8.9).
limitations_bias: Online recruitment may have attracted participants more familiar with technology; relatively small sample size; snowball/social media recruitment limits representativeness and generalizability; benefits and harms may be underestimated because use may have hidden or delayed effects; cross-sectional self-report design prevents causal inference.
relevance_to_our_review: Relevant as observational evidence on perceived effects of AI use on mental health support and associated harms/concerns, especially for generative AI/chatbots used in mental health contexts. However, it does not test clinical mental health outcomes or causal effects of AI exposure.
reason_for_decision: Useful for background and mapping perceived benefits/harms of AI in mental health care, but not strong evidence for actual causal effects on mental health outcomes.
notes_for_research_question: This paper is most relevant for understanding real-world adoption and user-perceived positive and negative effects of AI in mental health care. Community members often used AI as quick emotional support or a pseudo-therapist, suggesting possible substitution for professional care. Outcomes are perceptions rather than measured changes in depression, anxiety, or other symptoms.
